lessons.title: Understanding Syllogism Statements
lessons.concept: A syllogism gives statements (premises) and asks which conclusions logically follow. Common statement forms: All A are B (universal affirmative), No A are B (universal negative), Some A are B (particular affirmative), Some A are not B (particular negative). Conclusions must follow from given statements only, not from real-world assumptions.
lessons.formula: Validity rule: a conclusion is valid only if it is necessarily true in every diagram/case consistent with all premises.
lessons.worked_example: Statements: All cats are animals. All animals are living beings. Conclusion: All cats are living beings. This follows because the set of cats is inside animals, and animals inside living beings.
mistakes: Using outside knowledge instead of only the given statements
Assuming 'Some A are B' means 'Some A are not B' (it does not necessarily)
Reversing statements incorrectly (All A are B does not imply All B are A)

lessons.title: Venn Diagram Method
lessons.concept: Venn diagrams represent sets and relationships visually. 'All A are B' places A entirely inside B. 'No A are B' keeps A and B separate. 'Some A are B' shows overlap (at least one element common). To test a conclusion, see if any valid diagram can make it false; if yes, conclusion does not follow.
lessons.formula: Test by possibility: if a conclusion can be false in any case allowed by premises, it is not a definite conclusion.
lessons.worked_example: Statements: Some pens are books. All books are papers. Valid conclusion: Some pens are papers (the pens that are books must be papers). Not definite: All pens are papers (some pens may be outside books).
mistakes: Drawing only one convenient diagram and ignoring other valid arrangements
Treating 'some' as 'some but not all' unless stated
Missing the minimum overlap implied by chaining statements

lessons.title: Common Valid and Invalid Patterns
lessons.concept: Chaining works when the middle term connects sets properly: All A are B and All B are C implies All A are C. But All A are B and All C are B does not imply any relation between A and C. 'Some' statements give limited definite conclusions; check carefully for what must be true versus what may be true.
lessons.formula: Valid chain: A subset of B, B subset of C => A subset of C. Invalid conversion: All A are B !=> All B are A.
lessons.worked_example: Statements: All roses are flowers. Some flowers fade quickly. Conclusion 'Some roses fade quickly' is not definite because the fading flowers may be non-rose flowers.
mistakes: Assuming the converse of an 'All' statement
Forcing a definite conclusion when only possibility exists
Confusing 'Some A are not B' with 'No A are B'

practice.question: Statements: All dogs are animals. All animals breathe. Conclusion: All dogs breathe.
practice.explanation: Dogs are a subset of animals, and animals are a subset of beings that breathe. Therefore every dog must breathe.

practice.question: Statements: All apples are fruits. All fruits are sweet. Conclusion: All sweet things are apples.

options.D: Conclusion is definitely false by premises

practice.explanation: Premises imply apples are inside sweet things, but other sweet things may exist that are not apples. The converse does not follow.

practice.question: Statements: Some cats are black. All black things are dark. Conclusion: Some cats are dark.
practice.explanation: The cats that are black must also be dark because all black things are dark. So at least those cats are dark.

practice.question: Statements: No birds are mammals. All sparrows are birds. Conclusion: No sparrows are mammals.
practice.explanation: Sparrows are entirely within birds, and birds have no overlap with mammals. Therefore sparrows cannot be mammals.

practice.explanation: Coins are entirely inside metals, and metals have no overlap with stones, so no coin can be a stone. This follows by chaining a universal negative with a universal affirmative.

questions.question: Statements: All managers are employees. Some employees are trainees. Conclusions: I. Some managers are trainees. II. Some employees are managers.
questions.explanation: Since all managers are employees, there are definitely employees who are managers (II follows). Trainees among employees may or may not include managers, so I does not definitely follow.
questions.provenance: Authored original question; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.
